So Fe-rich films with a hematite/FeVO4-type absorber should absorb at 455 nm. Index 145 has the highest Fe content in the library.

content.text:
I submitted index 120 (Fe 0.56, Ni 0.21, V 0.23). At 5.5e-7 A, it had the highest photocurrent of the three compositions I measured.

| Index | Composition (Fe / Ni / V) | Photocurrent |
|---|---|---|
| 120 | 0.56 / 0.21 / 0.23 | **5.5e-7 A** |
| 145 | 0.62 / 0.22 / 0.16 (most Fe-rich in the library) | 4.8e-7 A |
| 115 | 0.32 / 0.18 / 0.50 (V-rich, FeVO4-like) | 2.1e-7 A |

The Fe-rich region clearly beat the V-rich region. That fits an iron oxide (hematite-type) absorber taking up the 2.72 eV light. Adding a little V while keeping Ni low gave a small gain over the most Fe-rich point.

The library has 200 compositions and I measured only 3, so there is no way to tell how close index 120 is to the true best. The Ni-rich region was never measured; I skipped it because nickel oxide's band gap is thought to be too wide to absorb at 455 nm.

- **Model checks were only a rough guide.** The full phase list was too large to read here, so I couldn't get its phase IDs. I used standard IDs for hematite and V2O5 (mp-19770, mp-25279) to get the band-gap receipts each measurement needs. My first guessed ID failed.
- **Choices came from chemistry knowledge plus the Gaussian-process suggestion.** The model's figures were used only to confirm the bulk oxides can absorb at this light energy. No mixed Fe-Ni-V phase was modelled.
- **No XRD was used** (0 of 5), so the phases in the measured films were not identified.
